figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Given a reference style image (a) and an input image (b), we seek to create an output image of the same scene as the input, but with the style of the reference image. The Neural Style algorithm [5] (c) successfully transfers colors, but also introduces distortions that make the output look like a painting, which is undesirable in the context of photo style transfer. In comparison, our result (d) transfers the color of the reference style image equally well while preserving the photorealism of the output. On the right (e), we show 3 insets of (b), (c), and (d) (in that order). Zoom in to compare results.
figures.headline: Neural Style transfers colors but adds painting-like distortion, while the proposed result transfers equally well and stays photorealistic.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Given an input image (a) and a reference style image (e), the results (b) of Gatys et al. [5] (Neural Style) and (c) of Li et al. [10] (CNNMRF) present artifacts due to strong distortions when compared to (d) our result. In (f,g,h), we compute the correspondence between the output and the reference style where, for each pixel, we encode the $XY$ coordinates of the nearest patch in the reference style image as a color with $(R,G,B)=(0,\,255\times Y/\mathrm{height},\,255\times X/\mathrm{width})$. The nearest neural patch is found using the L2 norm on the neural responses of the VGG-19 conv3_1 layer, similarly to CNNMRF. Neural Style computes global statistics of the reference style image which tends to produce texture mismatches as shown in the correspondence (f), e.g., parts of the sky in the output image map to the buildings from the reference style image. CNNMRF computes a nearest-neighbor search of the reference style image which tends to have many-to-one mappings as shown in the correspondence (g), e.g., see the buildings. In comparison, our result (d) prevents distortions and matches the texture correctly as shown in the correspondence (h).
figures.headline: Competing methods show distortion and mismatched correspondences, while the proposed result avoids distortion and matches texture correctly.
citing_sentences: These issues are demonstrated in Figure 2.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Transferring the dramatic appearance of the reference style image ((a)-inset), onto an ordinary flat shot in (a) is challenging. We produce results using our method with different $\lambda$ parameters. A too small $\lambda$ value cannot prevent distortions, and thus the results have a non-photorealistic look in (b,c). Conversely, a too large $\lambda$ value suppresses the style to be transferred yielding a half-transferred look in (e,f). We found the best parameter $\lambda=10^{4}$ to be the sweet spot to produce our result (d) and all the other results in this paper.
figures.headline: A too-small regularization weight leaves distortion and a too-large one suppresses the style, with an intermediate weight giving the best result.
citing_sentences: The effect of $\lambda$ is illustrated in Figure 3.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Comparison of our method against Neural Style and CNNMRF. Both Neural Style and CNNMRF produce strong distortions in their synthesized images. Neural Style also entirely ignores the semantic context for style transfer. CNNMRF tends to ignore most of the texture in the reference style image since it uses nearest neighbor search. Our approach is free of distortions and matches texture semantically.
figures.headline: Neural Style and CNNMRF produce strong distortions, while the proposed method is free of distortions and matches texture semantically.
citing_sentences: We compare our method with Gatys et al. [5] (Neural Style for short) and Li et al. [10] (CNNMRF for short) across a series of indoor and outdoor scenes in Figure 4.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Comparison of our method against Reinhard et al. [12] and Pitié [11]. Our method provides more flexibility in transferring spatially-variant color changes, yielding better results than previous techniques.
figures.headline: Compared with the global methods of Reinhard and Pitié, the proposed method gives better results for spatially varying color changes.
citing_sentences: In Figure 5, we compare our method with global style transfer methods that do not distort images, Reinhard et al. [12] and Pitié et al. [11].

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Our method and the techique of Shih et al. [15] generate visually satisfying results. However, our algorithm requires a single style image instead of a full time-lapse video, and it can handle other scenarios in addition to time-of-day hallucination.
figures.headline: The proposed method and the time-of-day method of Shih both give visually satisfying but drastically different results.
citing_sentences: In Figure 6, we compare our method with the time-of-day hallucination of Shih et al. [15].

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Manual segmentation enables diverse tasks such as transferring a fireball (b) to a perfume bottle (a) to produce a fire-illuminated look (c), or switching the texture between different apples (d, e).
figures.headline: Manual segmentation lets users transfer a fireball's look onto a perfume bottle or swap textures between apples.
citing_sentences: In Figure 7, we show how users can control the transfer results simply by providing the semantic masks.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Failure cases due to extreme mismatch.
figures.headline: Failure cases appear under extreme mismatch between the input and reference content.
citing_sentences: In Figure 8, we show examples of failure due to extreme mismatch.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: User study results confirming that our algorithm produces photorealistic and faithful results.
figures.headline: User studies rank the method below histogram transfer on photorealism but most often pick it as the most faithful style match.
citing_sentences: Figure 9a shows that CNNMRF and Neural Style produce nonphotorealistic results, which confirms our observation that these techniques introduce painting-like distortions.

abstract: This paper introduces a deep-learning approach to photographic style transfer that handles a large variety of image content while faithfully transferring the reference style. Our approach builds upon the recent work on painterly transfer that separates style from the content of an image by considering different layers of a neural network. However, as is, this approach is not suitable for photorealistic style transfer. Even when both the input and reference images are photographs, the output still exhibits distortions reminiscent of a painting. Our contribution is to constrain the transformation from the input to the output to be locally affine in colorspace, and to express this constraint as a custom fully differentiable energy term. We show that this approach successfully suppresses distortion and yields satisfying photorealistic style transfers in a broad variety of scenarios, including transfer of the time of day, weather, season, and artistic edits.

sections.body: The section sets out the problem: existing methods are limited either in the scenes they handle or in how faithfully they match the reference style. The authors start from the Neural Style method, but its outputs still look like paintings, with straight edges becoming wiggly. They constrain the transformation to be locally affine in colorspace, expressed as a differentiable energy term inspired by the Matting Laplacian. The section states that this suppresses distortion with minimal impact on transfer faithfulness. A second contribution uses semantic segmentation of the input and reference images to stop style from spilling into unrelated content. Figure 2 illustrates these artifacts.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Photographic style transfer must avoid painting-like distortion while keeping the reference style faithful.

sections.body: The method starts from Neural Style and adds two terms. The first is a photorealism regularizer that penalizes outputs not explained by a locally affine color transform of the input, written as $\mathcal{L}_{m}=\sum_{c=1}^{3}V_{c}[O]^{T}\mathcal{M}_{I}V_{c}[O]$, where $\mathcal{M}_{I}$ is the Matting Laplacian of the input. The second is semantic guidance: style Gram matrices are computed per segmentation channel, so content is matched between corresponding regions. Input labels are restricted to labels present in the reference image. The total objective combines content, augmented style and regularization losses, with a weight lambda controlling the regularizer. The section states that segmentation need not be pixel accurate because the output is constrained by the regularizer.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: The method adds a locally affine color regularizer and semantic segmentation masks to Neural Style optimization.

sections.body: This section lists the settings used for all results. A pretrained VGG-19 network serves as the feature extractor. Content is represented at `conv4_2` and style at `conv1_1` through `conv5_1`, with the style weight `Gamma = 10^2` and the regularization weight $\lambda=10^{4}$. Optimization runs in two stages: the Neural Style output with the augmented style loss initializes the solver, which the authors say works better than solving the full objective directly. Segmentation uses DilatedNet, which recognizes 150 categories. The authors found this fine-grained set unnecessary and unstable, so they merged similar classes such as lake, river, ocean and water. The regularization gradient is implemented in CUDA.
sections.heading: Implementation Details
sections.headline: The implementation uses a pretrained convolutional network, two-stage optimization and merged segmentation classes.

sections.body: Visual comparisons in Figure 4 show painting-like distortion for Neural Style and CNNMRF. Neural Style also shows spillovers, such as sky taking the ground's style, and CNNMRF gives partial transfers that ignore parts of the style image. Figure 5 compares against the global methods of Reinhard and Pitié, which cannot handle spatially varying color changes. Figure 6 contrasts with time-of-day hallucination, which needs a full time-lapse video, while this method needs one style photo. The first user study rated photorealism on a 1-to-4 scale across 8 scenes and 4 methods, 32 questions in total, with 40 responses per question on average. The second study had 20 comparisons with 35 responses per question on average. Runtime is 3˜5 minutes on an NVIDIA Titan X GPU.
sections.heading: Results and Comparison
sections.headline: Compared with Neural Style, patch-based and global transfer methods, the approach avoids distortion and was judged most faithful more than 80% of the time.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the contribution. The method uses the Matting Laplacian to constrain the transformation to be locally affine in colorspace. Semantic segmentation guides the transfer toward more meaningful correspondences between regions. The authors report photorealistic results across time of day, weather, season and artistic edits. The section adds no new experiments and states no further limitations.
sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.headline: The approach transfers reference style faithfully across time of day, weather, season and artistic edits while keeping outputs photorealistic.
